doc.title: Stanley Kay interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Buddy Rich's broken arm and trouble reading music
summary: A handball game in Columbus, Ohio breaks Rich's arm, and he plays the Apollo and Paramount with a sling and two bass drums; Kay also tells of Rich and the drum book.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah, I heard something about that.
Well I know, you want to hear how it happened?

Okay we are in Ohio. And I’d sit next to him on the bus see. Right here. And then he had the outside, I had the window. But you know you’re doing 200 miles and you’ve got to —ah you’re disturbing me. I said, “wait a minute, you don’t want me to breathe?” Because I’d get into that with him. So we get into a town at eight in the morning, in Ohio. Columbus, Ohio. He said, “come on, let’s go to a movie.” He loved movies. Cowboy movies, D movies, E movies, Z’s, whatever they were. I said, “I’m not going to the movies today.” I said, “I’m going to the gym instead and I’m playing handball.” “I’m coming too,” he said. And his brother came, Nicky. We’re playing four wall handball. I don’t want to be the handball champ, I just want to hit the ball against the wall. But he’s got to be the best and he’s smashing it. But he ran into the wall like that. And he went ahh. So I said, “ah what? What are you singing?” So he said, “I think — my arm.” I said well go down and get a steam” they had a steam room there, a sauna, “and your brother and I will finish the game.” He comes back up. “My arm doesn’t feel good.” So I take him to the doctor. They put one of these slings on it, right? And we’re rooming together. And ah, at four in the morning, “my arm,” like a hypochondriac. So I says, “hey B listen,” I was straw boss of the band. “I got to get things going at seven in the morning. I can’t hear this all night.” But I said, “I’ll tell you something, if you die, I promise you I’ll make you a nice funeral. Let me get a little rest here.” I said, “I mess things up and then you’re going to get on me, ‘you don’t know what you’re doing,’ and I’m not going for that.” So anyway, we got three days left then we’re going to New York. We’ve got two days and we open at the Apollo Theater. He gets to New York and the arm was broken in three places. And he had like a brown suit, a brown sling, a gray suit, a gray –. He liked all that coordination. We opened the Apollo Theater — we were one of the favorites, and one of the few white bands that could do it. They liked Charlie Barnet and us. And he was a big favorite. So Tiny Kahn wrote a chart for us on the “Carioca.” I remember. See but he sits very high, and the layman don’t know if he’s playing with one hand or two hands. But [scats] but they don’t see it. They saw it when he came down to announce the

act and I played. They see the big sling. Clark Terry told me, he said he was there and the word went out that Buddy’s arm is not broken, he wants to show he can play with one hand. But it was broken. So we played there a week, then we go into the Paramount Theater downtown and the managing director of the Paramount, Bob Whiteman, came up. And he said, “the rumor is that your arm is not broken but there’s a sensation — keep it in the sling.” If it’s not broken we could play the Paramount. See and he never liked two bass drums. He said, “Louie’s jive with it. It’s tough enough to play one.” But they were good friends, don’t get me wrong. He said, “call Ludwig. Send for two bass drums.” So he could get anything he wants. So two bass drums come in. Never practiced it, sat on a stool, no other drums around him, and just played the two bass drums like a tap dancer. With the arm broken and everything. But here’s the uncanny part of this whole thing. Now if you’re an athlete, and your arm is, you know a pitcher or — but your arm is sprained, you don’t throw the ball fast like the 90 mile an hour fast ball, right? You work it in. The next day he took the thing off he played like it was never broken. And I just said I don’t know where that’s coming from. And that’s what he did. That’s what he did. And another story, see he always felt the guys were putting him down because he couldn’t read music. I mean he didn’t know a note. He was like Erroll Garner. Wherever the hands went was the key. So they wrote a book for him, The Drum Book, Henry Aller. And it sold like a hundred thousand copies, but everybody wanted the dexterity that Buddy had. So he decides to want to read. And he gets the drum pad. And his band boy was a drummer. You know, an amateur but he could read some. So Buddy opens the book and it’s page one, and he’s got to play four quarter notes and — two bars of four quarter and two bars of eighth notes. He could play the four quarter notes, he’s going right, left, right, left, right. But he can’t play one and two and, see he doesn’t understand that. And he was impatient. So after four or five minutes he took the book and threw it up against the wall, he said the book is wrong. That was him. And then the other part, a kid comes, he did a one day theater. He was very quick, quick humor. He was walking out on stage. Buddy was in a good mood, and the kid comes with a book like this, and he’s on page 110. Difficult. Not page one, page 110. And he goes, “Mr. Rich,” he says, “I’m a big fan of yours.” He says, “excuse me,” he says, “I’m having trouble with this passage.” And he goes “can you tell me how to play that?” He says, “just like it’s written, kid, just like it’s written” and walked away from him. So that was the humor.
